newsitem.title: USA: "Christmas miracle" cited in New Orleans shipwreck.
newsitem.headline: "Christmas miracle" cited in New Orleans shipwreck.

text.p: Officials on Monday credited a "Christmas miracle" as they expressed growing confidence that no one was killed when a giant freighter slammed into a riverside shopping mall on Saturday.

Rescue teams continued to search for possible victims but had found none in the rubble of a shopping centre and hotel that were badly damaged when the 735-foot (224 metre) ship Bright Field ran into the Mississippi River bank near the city's French Quarter.

Port of New Orleans director Ron Brinson told a news conference it looked increasingly likely there were no fatalities. "With each passing hour our confidence grows that in fact we do have a Christmas miracle and that we will get through this without any fatalities," he said.

New Orleans Fire Chief Warren McDaniels told reporters sensitive listening devices used in mine cave-ins and earthquake rescues had been brought in to help in the search. Infrared imaging equipment had turned up nothing, he said.
"We have no reason to believe there's anyone in the rubble, however we are not going to stop until we have searched every portion of that rubble," he told reporters.
Brinson said officials had received overnight reports of two people possibly missing in the crash but both had been found elsewhere by New Orleans police.

National Transportation Safety Board investigator John Hammerschmidt said only three of the 116 people treated for injuries in the incident were known still to be in hospitals, two with pelvic fractures and one with "abdominal trauma."

Many of the injuries occurred when people fled the area, known as the Riverwalk, as the ship drifted toward shore. The shopping mall located on the wharf, 125 rooms in the nearby New Orleans Hilton hotel and an adjacent parking garage were damaged by the ship.

Hammerschmidt said the Liberian-flagged Bright Field, with a cargo of 64,000 short tons of corn, rammed into the bank when its oil pump lost pressure and the pilot was unable to steer the ship. He said a backup oil pump and automatic control system came on as they were supposed to, but the control system reduced the engine's speed, which cut the ship's manuverability.

River pilot Ted Davisson, who was at the ship's helm, used what little control he had to avoid two docked cruise ships with 1,700 passengers and a riverboat casino loaded with 800 gamblers, thus saving many lives, officials said.

Davisson also dropped the ship's anchor to slow its speed and sounded its emergency horn to alert those in harm's way to flee. An amateur videotape of the crash showed the Bright Field ploughing up cement and people running for their lives as the ship ground along the wharf.
The Riverwalk is a few blocks from the edge of the French Quarter, the hub of New Orleans tourism.
Coast Guard Capt. Gordon Marsh said crewmembers of the ship were being interviewed but that a formal inquiry into the accident would not begin until Tuesday.

Hammerschmidt said the incident would be examined with an eye toward any problems in crew coordination and for any role that language difficulties may have played. The master of the vessel was Chinese and spoke no English, he said.

The ship, as it had been since Saturday, was being held in place by tugboats while rescue efforts continued. Officials said the freighter was holding up part of the shopping mall or the adjacent wharf.

A strong cold front that brought wind and rain was making the tugboats' task more difficult, officials said. But Brinson said operations in the New Orleans port, which had been affected by the crash, would return to normal within 24 hours.
Even as authorities tried to assess the damage, the first lawsuit against the ship's owner, the Cosco Co. of Hong Kong, was filed on Sunday in federal court in New Orleans.

Walter Lejier, one of eight attorneys filing the suit, said the plaintiffs include several Riverwalk business owners, residents of One River Place condominiums who had to leave their homes because utility connections were severed, and the owner of a car that fell from a parking garage into the river.
